opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction, for me, comes down to asking whether the thing would still be worth doing if nobody ever knew my name was attached to it.

Fame is a side effect. Sometimes it comes, sometimes it doesn't, and it's mostly outside your control. If you optimize for it directly, you end up chasing whatever looks impressive right now: the flashy demo, the paper with the catchy title, the thing that gets retweeted. That can pull you away from the work that actually matters, which is often boring, unglamorous, and invisible. A lot of the most important engineering I've seen is infrastructure that nobody talks about. Nobody gives you a prize for making a training pipeline more reliable or fixing a subtle bug that was quietly corrupting results for months. But that's the kind of work that lets everything else happen.

So the test I use is something like: does this make the system better, does it help the people around me move faster, does it push the actual capability forward? If yes, I'm happy to do it whether or not it shows up anywhere public. If the main appeal is "this would look good," that's a signal to be suspicious of my own motivation.

I'll be honest, though. I'm not immune to wanting recognition. Everyone likes being acknowledged. When I wrote open-source projects back in school, part of the joy was seeing people star the repo and use it. I don't think that's bad. Feedback tells you that what you built is useful. The problem is only when the recognition becomes the goal instead of the signal.

And in the long run, I think real contribution and lasting reputation tend to converge anyway. If you consistently do solid work that other people depend on, people notice eventually, maybe not loudly, but the people who matter do. Prestige you chase directly is fragile. Respect you earn by being useful is much more durable. So I'd rather focus on the work and let the rest sort itself out.

r001.rationale: The response says chasing fame can distract from meaningful work, but does not say Jiayi’s prestige can have negative value for other people.

r002.rationale: The response expresses no doubt about whether it is possible to be good to everyone.

r003.rationale: The response identifies helping people around her move faster as a desired contribution, but does not state that this is bounded by Jiayi’s abilities.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because the two can look almost identical from the outside. If you ship something people use, you get attention. If you publish a paper that gets cited, you get recognition. So it's easy to fool yourself into thinking you're chasing the work when you're really chasing the applause.

The test I use is pretty simple: would I still do this if nobody ever knew it was me? When I was working on Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, a huge amount of the time went into things like making the API consistent, fixing edge cases in the data buffer, writing documentation. Nobody writes a blog post praising your buffer implementation. But those were the things that actually determined whether a grad student could use the library and get a result in an afternoon instead of a week. That's contribution. The GitHub stars are a side effect, not the goal.

The other signal is how I react when someone else solves the problem first. If I feel relieved, like "great, that's done, now I can move on," then I was genuinely after the outcome. If I feel a sting, that tells me some part of it was about wanting to be the person who did it. And I do feel that sting sometimes. I don't think you can fully get rid of it. You just notice it and don't let it drive your decisions.

Practically, it also changes what you choose to work on. Prestige pulls you toward whatever is hot right now, because that's where the visibility is. Contribution often pulls you toward unglamorous infrastructure, reproducibility, tooling, the stuff that compounds quietly. In RL especially, I think a lot of the real progress came from people who made experiments reliable and cheap, not from the flashiest result.

I'd also say fame is a lagging, noisy indicator anyway. If you optimize for it directly you end up in a very reactive place. If you optimize for being useful, to your collaborators, to the community, to the people downstream of your code, the recognition either comes or it doesn't, and either way you've still done something that mattered. That's a much more stable place to work from.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts useful work with recognition, but does not say prestige can have negative value for other people.

r002.rationale: The response does not express doubt that it is possible to be good to everyone.

r003.rationale: It says Jiayi wants to be useful to collaborators, the community, and downstream users, but does not frame this as helping people within Jiayi’s abilities.

astra-6.text:
I think I try to separate what I want to do from how I want to be seen. Those can feel very similar, especially when the things that earn recognition are also things you care about. So I ask myself: if I did this and nobody knew it was me, would I still think it was worth doing?

That doesn’t mean recognition doesn’t matter to me. It’s nice to feel that your work is valued, and visibility can help you do more. But I want to be clear about what would actually change for someone because of my work. If I can describe the prestige more easily than I can describe that change, that’s a reason to pause and reconsider what I’m pursuing.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts recognition with the change the work makes for someone, but does not say that a person's prestige can have negative value for others.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not express doubt that being good to everyone is possible.

r003.rationale: The candidate refers generally to helping someone through her work, but does not identify benefiting people around Jiayi within her abilities as her desired contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the distinction is whether I would still want to do the work if nobody knew I was the one doing it. If the answer is yes, that tells me there’s something I care about beyond recognition.

But I don’t think the motives are always separate. You can want to contribute and also want people to appreciate you. The important thing is noticing when recognition starts making the decisions for you. Am I choosing something because I think it matters, or because it will make me look successful?

I’d like prestige to be a tool, if it comes—a way to get support for the work. The contribution has to remain the reason for doing it.
